mcqs.question: Which statement correctly states the principle of superposition for waves?

options.A: When two waves overlap, the resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements at that point.
options.B: When two waves overlap, they cancel each other completely regardless of their phase relationship.
options.C: The resultant displacement is the product of the individual displacements of the overlapping waves.
options.D: Only the wave with the larger amplitude determines the resultant displacement.

mcqs.answer: When two waves overlap, the resultant displacement at any point is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements at that point.
mcqs.explanation: The principle of superposition states that at any point where two or more waves meet, the total displacement is the vector (algebraic) sum of the individual displacements. Option B is a common misconception that waves always cancel, which is false. Option C incorrectly suggests multiplication, and Option D ignores the contribution of the smaller wave. Therefore, option A correctly describes the principle.

mcqs.question: Two coherent waves of equal amplitude interfere constructively. If each wave has an amplitude of 5 cm, what is the amplitude of the resultant wave?
mcqs.explanation: In constructive interference the displacements add in phase, so the resultant amplitude equals the sum of the individual amplitudes: 5 cm + 5 cm = 10 cm. Option A would be the case for no interference, C corresponds to complete destructive interference, and D is unrelated.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly compares destructive interference with constructive interference for two waves of equal amplitude?

options.A: In destructive interference the resultant amplitude is zero, whereas in constructive interference it is twice the individual amplitude.
options.B: Destructive interference results in an amplitude twice the individual amplitude, while constructive interference results in zero amplitude.
options.C: Both destructive and constructive interference always give zero resultant amplitude.
options.D: Both destructive and constructive interference always give twice the individual amplitude.

mcqs.answer: In destructive interference the resultant amplitude is zero, whereas in constructive interference it is twice the individual amplitude.
mcqs.explanation: When two equal‑amplitude waves are exactly out of phase (phase difference 180°), their displacements cancel, giving zero resultant amplitude – destructive interference. When they are in phase (phase difference 0°), the amplitudes add, giving twice the individual amplitude – constructive interference. Options B, C, and D invert or ignore these facts.

mcqs.question: Two coherent waves of the same frequency and amplitude travel in the same direction. What phase difference between them will produce the first minimum (destructive interference) in the resultant intensity?
mcqs.explanation: Destructive interference occurs when the two waves are half a wavelength out of phase, i.e., a phase difference of 180°. This causes the peaks of one wave to align with the troughs of the other, cancelling the resultant displacement. 0° and 360° give constructive interference, while 90° gives partial (neither maximum nor minimum) interference.
